title: Finding the Old Stories
bigQuestion: How do we know what matches were like long ago?

story.title: A New Book on the Table
story.kicker: A teacher opens a book full of old pictures and old rules.
paragraphs: It is reading time. A teacher opens a big book on the rug. The first page shows a painting on a stone wall. Two wrestlers reach for each other.
The painting is about four thousand years old. It comes from a tomb in Egypt. The children lean in close. How can a picture last so long?
The next page shows an old rule book. Then a photo of a museum in Tokyo. Each page holds a clue about the past. The children count three kinds of clues.
History is like a puzzle. Pictures, books, records and places are the pieces. People who study history put the pieces together.
story.think: What old thing in your home could tell a story about the past?

lessons.title: Wrestlers on a Tomb Wall
lessons.mainIdea: Paintings in Egyptian tombs show that wrestling is very old.
reading: Beni Hasan is a place in Egypt, near the Nile River. People carved tombs into the cliffs there about four thousand years ago.
Painters covered the tomb walls with pictures. One wall shows many pairs of *wrestlers*. Each pair is shown in a different pose.
These *paintings* are clues. They tell us people in Egypt wrestled long, long ago.

words.d: people who take part in wrestling
pictures made with paint; old ones are clues about the past

look.title: Rows on a Wall
look.text: Look at a long stone wall inside a cliff. Rows of small painted people cover it. In each row, two people hold on to each other. The paint is red, brown and black.
look.prompt: What can a picture tell us, even when no one wrote words?

check.why: Beni Hasan is in Egypt, near the Nile River.

check.q: What do the Beni Hasan tomb walls show?
check.why: One wall shows many pairs of wrestlers.

check.q: About how old are the Beni Hasan tombs?
check.why: The tombs were made about four thousand years ago.

lessons.title: Pictures on Greek Pots
lessons.mainIdea: Old Greek pots show wrestling and boxing at the ancient games.
reading: Long ago, people in Greece held games at a place called Olympia. These were the *ancient Olympics*. They were held every four years.
Greek writers said wrestling joined the games in 708 BCE. Boxing joined in 688 BCE. Artists painted these sports on clay *pots*. Many of those pots are in museums today.

words.d: the old games held at Olympia in Greece every four years
clay jars; Greek pots often had paintings on them

look.title: When Sports Joined the Ancient Games
look.unit: year BCE (dates told by Greek writers)
look.cite: Dates as given by ancient Greek writers, reported in histories of the ancient Olympics
look.prompt: Which sport joined the games first?

check.q: Where were the ancient Olympics held?
check.why: The ancient Olympics were held at Olympia in Greece.

check.q: What did Greek artists paint sports on?
check.why: Greek artists painted sports on clay pots.

check.q: Which sport joined the ancient games first?
check.why: Greek writers said wrestling joined in 708 BCE, before boxing in 688 BCE.

lessons.title: Kano Writes It Down
lessons.mainIdea: Kano Jigoro wrote down his ideas, so we can read how judo began.
reading: Kano Jigoro started judo in 1882. He was also a school teacher. He wrote many talks and articles about judo.
He wrote about two big ideas. One means best use of energy. The other means helping each other so all do well. Judo schools still teach these *ideas*.
Because Kano *wrote* things down, we can read his own words today. Judo teachers in many countries still read them.

words.d: put words on paper so others could read them later
thoughts about how to live or what matters

look.title: Two Ideas of Judo
look.text: Kano named two ideas for judo: use your energy in the best way, and help each other so that everyone does well.
look.cite: Kano Jigoro, writings on judo, early 1900s
look.prompt: Which idea is about helping others?

check.q: What other job did Kano Jigoro have?
check.why: Kano Jigoro was also a school teacher.

check.q: Why can we read Kano's ideas today?
check.why: Kano wrote talks and articles, so his words were kept.

check.q: Which is one of Kano's two ideas?
choices: help each other so all do well
check.why: One of Kano's ideas is helping each other so that everyone does well.

lessons.title: Olympic Records
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic records tell us the year each sport joined the modern games.
reading: The *International Olympic Committee* keeps careful lists. They show which sports were in each Olympics. These lists are called *records*.
The records show that judo joined in 1964, in Tokyo. Women's judo joined in 1992, in Barcelona. Taekwondo joined in 2000, in Sydney.

words.d: careful written lists of what happened and when
the group that runs the modern Olympic Games

look.title: Joining the Olympics
look.cite: International Olympic Committee, Olympic Games results
look.prompt: Which sport joined the Olympics first?

check.q: In what city did judo join the Olympics?
check.why: Judo joined the Olympics in Tokyo in 1964.

check.q: When did women's judo join the Olympics?
check.why: Olympic records show women's judo joined in 1992 in Barcelona.

choices: a careful written list of what happened
check.why: Records are careful lists of what happened and when.

lessons.title: A Legend in an Old Book
lessons.mainIdea: An old book from Japan tells a sumo legend, a story we cannot prove.
reading: The Nihon Shoki is an old book of Japan. It was finished in the year 720. It tells a story about two strong men in a match.
Many people call this the first sumo match. But it is a *legend*. A legend is an old story that no one can prove. *Historians* keep legends and proof apart.

words.d: an old story that is told again and again but cannot be proved
people who study the past and check the clues

look.title: Story or Proof?
look.text: Two things sit on a table. One is an old book with a story of two strong men long ago. The other is a list of sumo winners, written down year by year.
look.prompt: Which one is a legend, and which one is a record?

check.q: When was the Nihon Shoki finished?
check.why: The Nihon Shoki was finished in the year 720.

choices: an old story no one can prove
check.why: A legend is an old story that cannot be proved.

check.q: What do historians do with legends?
check.why: Historians keep legends apart from things they can prove.

lessons.title: Museums in Tokyo
lessons.mainIdea: Museums keep old objects so people can learn from them.
reading: A *museum* is a place that keeps old things safe. People visit to look and learn.
In Tokyo, the big sumo hall has a Sumo Museum. It keeps old prints, belts and banners. The Kodokan in Tokyo has a judo museum too. It tells the story of Kano and his school.

words.d: a place that keeps old or special objects safe for people to see
things you can see and touch, like belts, prints and pots

look.title: Behind the Glass
look.text: Look at a glass case in a quiet room. Inside is an old, wide belt with a thick rope. A small card sits beside it. The card tells who wore it and when.
look.prompt: What could the card beside the belt teach you?

check.why: A museum keeps old objects safe so people can learn.

check.q: Which city has a Sumo Museum?
check.why: The Sumo Museum is in the big sumo hall in Tokyo.

check.q: What does the judo museum at the Kodokan tell about?
check.why: The Kodokan judo museum tells the story of Kano and his school.

review.q: What do the Beni Hasan paintings show?
review.why: The Beni Hasan tomb paintings show many pairs of wrestlers.

review.q: What did Greek artists paint on pots?
review.why: Greek pots show sports from the ancient games.

review.q: Who wrote about the ideas of judo?
review.why: Kano Jigoro wrote talks and articles about judo.

review.q: What year did taekwondo join the Olympics?
review.why: Olympic records show taekwondo joined in 2000 in Sydney.

review.q: The first sumo match in the Nihon Shoki is a ...
review.why: It is a legend, an old story that cannot be proved.

review.q: Which of these is a clue about the past?
choices: a painting in an old tomb
review.why: Old paintings, books, records and objects are clues about the past.
